Question: A document-summarization service is deployed to App Service from `ttnacr.azurecr.io/summarizer:latest`, which the pipeline overwrites on every merge. Two instances of the same app now return different summaries for identical input, and a rollback attempt reproduced the newest behaviour rather than the previous one. What should the team change first?
Answer Option 1: Pin each deployment to an immutable, uniquely versioned tag (or the image digest) and lock the tag so it can never be overwritten
Explanation 1: Correct. A mutable `latest` tag means the bytes behind the tag change over time, so instances that pulled at different moments run different code and rollback has no earlier tag to return to. Versioned tags — optionally hardened with `az acr repository update --image summarizer:2026.04.1 --write-enabled false` — make deployments reproducible and rollback a matter of redeploying a known tag.
Answer Option 2: Enable the ACR retention policy for untagged manifests so old layers are purged and instances converge on one image
Explanation 2: Retention policies delete untagged manifests to control storage cost, which is useful housekeeping but irrelevant here. Purging old manifests would actually destroy the very images the team needs for rollback, making the situation worse rather than restoring determinism.
Answer Option 3: Scale the App Service plan out to more instances so a fresh pull happens on each worker after every merge
Explanation 3: Adding instances multiplies the problem instead of solving it: each new worker pulls whatever `latest` points to at its own start time, so the fleet can end up running three versions instead of two. Scaling is a capacity lever, not a versioning one.
Answer Option 4: Turn on ACR geo-replication so all App Service workers pull from a consistent regional replica of the registry
Explanation 4: Geo-replication reduces pull latency and improves availability for multi-region deployments, and Premium-tier replicas are eventually consistent copies of the same mutable tag. It does nothing about the fact that the tag itself keeps being reassigned to new content.
Overall Explanation: Mutable `latest` tags produce drift between instances and make rollback impossible. Deploy uniquely versioned, immutable tags or digests so every instance provably runs the same bytes.

Question: A compliance review found that the base image `python:3.12-slim` used by six inference services carries OS packages that are three months behind on security fixes, and nobody rebuilds unless application code changes. The team wants patched images produced automatically, without a developer running a build. Which two ACR Tasks capabilities address this? (Choose two.)
Answer Option 1: Create the task with base-image update triggers enabled so ACR rebuilds dependent images when the base image is updated
Explanation 1: Correct. A base-image update trigger is exactly the mechanism for this problem: ACR tracks the base image referenced in the Dockerfile and queues a rebuild of the dependent image when that base is updated, so patched images appear without human involvement.
Answer Option 2: Add a scheduled timer trigger to the task so the image is rebuilt on a recurring cadence regardless of source or base-image changes
Explanation 2: Correct. A timer trigger complements the base-image trigger by guaranteeing a floor on rebuild frequency, which matters when a fix arrives through a package repository rather than a new base-image push. Together the two triggers cover both event-driven and time-driven patching.
Answer Option 3: Enable the registry retention policy for untagged manifests so vulnerable layers are deleted after the configured number of days
Explanation 3: Retention policies control storage growth by deleting untagged manifests; deleting an old manifest does not produce a patched one. This confuses cleaning up the registry with refreshing the contents of the images it holds.
Answer Option 4: Switch the build to `docker build` on a self-hosted agent so the agent's local layer cache always resolves the newest base image
Explanation 4: Local layer caching pushes in the wrong direction — a warm cache is exactly what causes a stale base layer to be reused. It also reintroduces build agents to maintain, which is the operational burden ACR Tasks exists to remove.
Overall Explanation: Base-image update triggers rebuild dependents when the upstream image changes, and timer triggers guarantee a periodic refresh. Both are ACR Tasks features designed to automate patching.

Question: A 4 GB inference image lives in a registry in West Europe. A new App Service deployment in Australia East takes eleven minutes to pull on every cold start and scale-out event, while the West Europe deployment of the same image takes under a minute. The team wants pulls to be fast in both regions from one logical registry. What should you do?
Answer Option 1: Use a Premium-tier registry and add a geo-replication in Australia East so pulls are served from a local replica of the same registry
Explanation 1: Correct. Geo-replication is the Premium-tier feature built for exactly this: one registry name and one push, with content replicated to each configured region and pulls automatically served from the network-closest replica. Cross-continent transfer of a 4 GB image disappears from the cold-start path.
Answer Option 2: Create a second Basic registry in Australia East and have the pipeline run a separate `az acr build` against it after every release
Explanation 2: A second registry does remove the cross-region hop, but at the price of two registry names, two builds of the same source, and no guarantee the two artefacts are byte-identical. It reintroduces the drift problem that single-artefact promotion exists to prevent.
Answer Option 3: Enable the dedicated data endpoint on the existing registry so the Australia East workers negotiate a faster transfer protocol
Explanation 3: Dedicated data endpoints exist to give the registry's data plane stable, per-region hostnames so tight firewall rules can be written. They change which hostname serves the layers, not the physical distance the bytes must travel.
Answer Option 4: Increase the App Service plan tier in Australia East so the workers are allocated more network bandwidth for the pull
Explanation 4: A larger plan gives more CPU and memory, and instance bandwidth is not the bottleneck when the constraint is intercontinental latency and throughput to a single remote region. This treats a data-locality problem as a compute-sizing problem.
Overall Explanation: Geo-replicate the Premium registry into Australia East. One registry name and one push, with pulls served from the closest replica, is what fixes cross-region image pull times.

Question: A Python container serving Uvicorn on 0.0.0.0:8080 starts cleanly on App Service — the log shows "Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8080" — yet browsing the site returns a 502 and the platform log records that the container did not respond to HTTP pings on port 80. The Dockerfile has no `EXPOSE` instruction. What resolves this?
Answer Option 1: Add an app setting `WEBSITES_PORT=8080` so App Service forwards inbound traffic to the port the container actually listens on
Explanation 1: Correct. App Service defaults to port 80 for a custom container unless told otherwise, either by an `EXPOSE` instruction or by the `WEBSITES_PORT` app setting. Declaring 8080 makes the platform forward requests to the listening socket, and the ping succeeds immediately.
Answer Option 2: Change the container to listen on 127.0.0.1:8080 so only the platform's local health probe can reach the application
Explanation 2: Binding to loopback is the classic way to make a container unreachable: the platform's request forwarding arrives over the container's network interface, not from inside it. This would guarantee a permanent 502 rather than fix one.
Answer Option 3: Configure a custom health check path on the Web App so the platform probes `/healthz` instead of the container root
Explanation 3: A health check path is genuinely useful for taking unhealthy instances out of rotation once traffic flows, and pointing it at a cheap endpoint is good practice. But it changes the path being probed, not the port, so the platform would still probe the wrong port and see nothing.
Answer Option 4: Enable `WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE` so the platform can mount the shared filesystem the container needs before binding
Explanation 4: That setting controls whether the `/home` directory is mounted into the container for persistence and shared content. It has no bearing on which port the platform forwards traffic to, so the port mismatch would remain.
Overall Explanation: Set `WEBSITES_PORT=8080` (or add a matching `EXPOSE`). The application is healthy; App Service is simply probing the default port 80 instead of the one Uvicorn bound.

Question: The team wants a merge to `main` to result in the App Service running the new image automatically, with no deployment step in their build pipeline. The app runs `ttnacr.azurecr.io/chat-api:staging`, and the pipeline uses `az acr build` to rebuild that tag on every merge. What must be in place for the app to pick up the rebuilt image?
Answer Option 1: Set `DOCKER_ENABLE_CI=true` on the Web App and register the ACR webhook that notifies the app's deployment endpoint on push
Explanation 1: Correct. Continuous deployment for Web App for Containers is push-driven: `DOCKER_ENABLE_CI` opts the app in, and the registry webhook fires on the push that `az acr build` performs, prompting the app to pull the tag again. That is what closes the gap between the build step and a running deployment.
Answer Option 2: Enable Always On so the app periodically re-resolves the tag and restarts when the underlying digest changes
Explanation 2: Always On stops the app being unloaded when idle; it never re-resolves image tags or compares digests. The container image is resolved at start, so an idle-timeout setting cannot drive redeployment.
Answer Option 3: Enable the ACR retention policy so the previous manifest is deleted, which forces the app to re-pull on its next request
Explanation 3: Retention policies delete untagged manifests as housekeeping and have no signalling relationship with a running app. Deleting an old manifest also does not cause a running container to restart, so nothing would trigger a pull.
Answer Option 4: Turn on system-assigned managed identity for the Web App, which makes it poll the registry for new digests every five minutes
Explanation 4: Managed identity governs how the app authenticates to the registry, not whether it checks for new content. There is no polling behaviour attached to enabling an identity — deployment remains event-driven via the webhook.
Overall Explanation: Enable `DOCKER_ENABLE_CI` on the Web App and wire the ACR webhook so the push performed by `az acr build` triggers the app to pull the tag again.

Question: A containerized App Service app downloads 3 GB of model weights on every start, adding minutes to each scale-out and restart. The team wants the weights fetched once and shared by all instances of the app, without rebuilding the 300 MB application image into a multi-gigabyte one. What is the appropriate approach?
Answer Option 1: Mount an Azure Files share into the container as a path with `az webapp config storage-account add` and load the weights from the mount
Explanation 1: Correct. Bring-your-own-storage mounts an Azure Files share into the container at a chosen path, giving every instance the same durable copy of large assets. The image stays small and unchanged while the weights are fetched once and shared across scale-out.
Answer Option 2: Write the weights to `/tmp` on first start and have subsequent instances read them from there, since the plan's workers share that path
Explanation 2: `/tmp` is the container's own writable layer and is discarded when the container is replaced; it is not shared between instances. Each new instance would find an empty directory and download the weights again, which is exactly the current behaviour.
Answer Option 3: Copy the weights into the image with a `COPY` layer so the pull benefits from registry layer caching on every worker
Explanation 3: Baking the weights in does remove the runtime download, and layer reuse helps on a worker that already holds the layer, but it inflates every pull on a cold worker to multiple gigabytes and forces a full rebuild and redeploy whenever the weights change. It trades one slow path for another.
Answer Option 4: Store the weights as an App Service app setting so the platform injects them into the container at start-up
Explanation 4: App settings are environment variables intended for short configuration values, and they are size-limited and entirely unsuitable for binary model artefacts. This confuses configuration injection with data distribution.
Overall Explanation: Mount an Azure Files share into the container and read the weights from it. The image stays small, the download happens once, and every instance sees the same durable copy.

Question: An engineer updates the value of a Container Apps secret named `servicebus-conn` after a connection string rotation, and separately changes the `LOG_LEVEL` environment variable on the same app. They observe that one change produced a new revision and the other did not, and they want to understand the rule before writing the runbook. What is the correct explanation?
Answer Option 1: Environment-variable changes are revision-scope so they create a new revision, while secret values are application-scope and apply across revisions once containers restart
Explanation 1: Correct. Container Apps splits configuration into revision-scope changes — image, environment variables, resources, scale rules — which produce a new immutable revision, and application-scope changes such as secret values, ingress and Dapr settings, which apply to all revisions. A rotated secret therefore reaches running revisions once their replicas restart, without a revision bump.
Answer Option 2: Both changes are revision-scope, but secret updates reuse the existing revision name so the new revision is not visible in the revision list
Explanation 2: Revision names are unique and revisions are immutable, so a change that created one would always show up in `az containerapp revision list`. This explanation invents hidden revisions to reconcile the observation instead of accepting the two different scopes.
Answer Option 3: Both changes are application-scope; the new revision appeared because the container image digest was re-resolved during the update
Explanation 3: If both were application-scope, changing `LOG_LEVEL` would not have created a revision at all, so the premise fails immediately. Image digests are also not silently re-resolved on an unrelated configuration update.
Answer Option 4: Secret changes are revision-scope and environment-variable changes are application-scope, which is why the secret rotation forced the new revision
Explanation 4: This is the correct rule with the two categories swapped, which is the most common way the distinction is misremembered. Getting it backwards leads to a runbook that expects a revision bump on rotation and a silent update on env-var changes — the opposite of the real behaviour.
Overall Explanation: Environment variables, image, resources and scale rules are revision-scope and create a new revision; secrets, ingress and Dapr configuration are application-scope and apply across revisions.

Question: An AKS-hosted embedding service loads a model for roughly 150 seconds before it can serve. Pods enter `CrashLoopBackOff` shortly after start, and `kubectl describe pod` shows `Liveness probe failed: connection refused` followed by container restarts. The current manifest defines only a liveness probe with `initialDelaySeconds: 10` and `periodSeconds: 10`. Which two manifest changes fix this correctly? (Choose two.)
Answer Option 1: Add a `startupProbe` whose `failureThreshold` multiplied by `periodSeconds` comfortably exceeds the 150-second warm-up
Explanation 1: Correct. A startup probe exists precisely to protect slow-starting containers: while it is running, liveness and readiness checks are suspended, and only when it succeeds do they take over. Sizing `failureThreshold × periodSeconds` above the real warm-up gives the model time to load without the kubelet declaring the container dead.
Answer Option 2: Add a `readinessProbe` so the Service only sends traffic once the model has finished loading and the pod reports ready
Explanation 2: Correct. Liveness answers "should this container be restarted" while readiness answers "should this pod receive traffic", and the second question is unanswered in the current manifest. Without a readiness probe the Service would route requests to a pod that is still loading, producing connection errors for real users.
Answer Option 3: Remove the liveness probe entirely, since a container that has crashed will be restarted by the kubelet in any case
Explanation 3: Removing liveness leaves the deployment with no way to recover a hung-but-running process, which is the failure mode liveness exists to catch — a wedged worker that still holds its socket open is not a crash the kubelet would notice. The probe is not wrong here; its timing is.
Answer Option 4: Raise the liveness probe's `timeoutSeconds` to 150 so a single probe attempt waits out the model load
Explanation 4: `timeoutSeconds` bounds how long one probe attempt waits for a response, not how long the container may take to become responsive. With the connection actively refused, the attempt fails immediately regardless of the timeout, and restarts continue.
Overall Explanation: Add a startup probe sized above the true warm-up so liveness is suspended during loading, and add a readiness probe so traffic arrives only when the model is ready.

Question: A newly applied AKS Deployment leaves every pod in `ImagePullBackOff`. `kubectl describe pod` shows `Failed to pull image "ttnacr.azurecr.io/router:2026.05.2": 401 Unauthorized`. The image and tag exist in the registry, and a developer can pull it after `az acr login`. What is the appropriate fix?
Answer Option 1: Attach the registry to the cluster with `az aks update --attach-acr ttnacr` so the cluster's identity is granted AcrPull
Explanation 1: Correct. A 401 on pull means the node's kubelet has no credential for the registry: the developer's success only proves their own identity works. `az aks update --attach-acr` grants the cluster's kubelet identity the AcrPull role, after which pulls authenticate without any imagePullSecret in the manifest; `az aks check-acr` confirms the path end to end.
Answer Option 2: Recreate the pods with `kubectl rollout restart deployment/router`, since the nodes cached a stale authentication token
Explanation 2: Restarting the rollout recreates pods that will attempt the same unauthenticated pull and fail identically. It is a reasonable reflex for transient issues, but a missing role assignment is not transient — nothing about a restart creates a credential.
Answer Option 3: Add the registry hostname to the cluster's DNS configuration so nodes can resolve `ttnacr.azurecr.io`
Explanation 3: A DNS failure would surface as a resolution or connection error naming the host, not as an HTTP 401 from the registry. The 401 proves the node reached the registry and was refused on authentication grounds.
Answer Option 4: Rebuild and push the image with `az acr build` so the manifest is re-signed for the cluster's node pool
Explanation 4: Rebuilding produces a new image but changes nothing about who is allowed to pull it, and image manifests are not signed per node pool. The same 401 would follow the new tag.
Overall Explanation: A 401 on image pull means the cluster identity lacks AcrPull. Attach the registry with `az aks update --attach-acr` and verify with `az aks check-acr`.

Question: An AKS pod restarted twice overnight and the on-call engineer needs the Python traceback the process printed just before it died. Running `kubectl logs pod/scorer-7d9` returns only the current container's fresh startup lines, and the incident review requires evidence that survives pod deletion. Which combination should the engineer use?
Answer Option 1: `kubectl logs pod/scorer-7d9 --previous` for the terminated container, plus Container Insights so `ContainerLogV2` retains the output in Log Analytics
Explanation 1: Correct. `--previous` retrieves the log of the container instance that terminated, which is the only way to see the traceback that preceded the restart, and it is still lost once the pod object goes away. Container Insights ships stdout and stderr into the `ContainerLogV2` table in Log Analytics, giving the durable, queryable evidence the review needs.
Answer Option 2: `kubectl describe pod scorer-7d9` alone, since container stdout is included in the pod description alongside the events
Explanation 2: `kubectl describe` returns the pod's spec, status and recent events, which is invaluable for scheduling and probe failures but never includes container stdout. It would show that a restart happened without revealing why.
Answer Option 3: `kubectl exec -it pod/scorer-7d9 -- cat /var/log/app.log`, because the kubelet writes each container's stdout into the pod filesystem
Explanation 3: Container stdout is captured by the container runtime, not written to a file inside the container unless the application does so itself, and anything on the container filesystem is destroyed on restart anyway. `kubectl exec` also requires a running container, which is not where the evidence lives.
Answer Option 4: `az containerapp logs show --follow` against the cluster, which streams historical container output from the AKS control plane
Explanation 4: `az containerapp logs` targets Azure Container Apps resources and has no relationship with an AKS cluster. Using it here confuses two different container platforms' tooling.
Overall Explanation: Use `kubectl logs --previous` for the terminated container and rely on Container Insights writing to `ContainerLogV2` for evidence that outlives the pod.
Domain: Develop containerized solutions on Azure

Question: A re-embedding workload drains the `reindex` Service Bus queue. Each message takes about eight minutes, work arrives in unpredictable bursts a few times a week, and the container must exit when the batch is done rather than stay resident. The team is already using a Container Apps environment. What is the right construct?
Answer Option 1: An event-driven Azure Container Apps job with a Service Bus scale rule, which starts job executions when messages arrive and ends them on completion
Explanation 1: Correct. Container Apps jobs model run-to-completion work: an event-driven job uses a KEDA scale rule such as `azure-servicebus` to start executions when the queue has messages, runs each execution to completion, and stops. That matches bursty batch processing far better than a long-lived app that must be kept alive.
Answer Option 2: A container app with `minReplicas` 0 and an HTTP scale rule, invoked by a Logic App that calls its endpoint when a message arrives
Explanation 2: This bolts an external trigger onto a service designed to stay running, adds a Logic App to maintain, and leaves the work inside a request that must survive eight minutes. The platform already exposes the queue trigger natively through jobs.
Answer Option 3: A manual Container Apps job that an operator triggers with `az containerapp job start` whenever the queue is observed to be non-empty
Explanation 3: Manual jobs are the right construct for operator-initiated runs such as a one-off migration, but here the trigger is a queue that fills unpredictably. Requiring a human to notice the backlog defeats the purpose of event-driven processing.
Answer Option 4: A container app with a CPU scale rule and an eight-minute liveness probe timeout to keep the long-running container alive
Explanation 4: This keeps a service resident to do batch work and papers over the mismatch with probe tuning; a liveness timeout also does not extend how long a unit of work may run. The requirement explicitly says the container should exit when the batch completes.
Overall Explanation: Use an event-driven Container Apps job with a Service Bus scale rule. Jobs start on the event, run to completion and exit, which is exactly the lifecycle bursty batch work needs.

Question: A Container App must read an Azure OpenAI key as the environment variable `AZURE_OPENAI_KEY`, and the security team requires that the key lives only in Key Vault, is never visible in the app's configuration output, and is picked up on rotation without a redeploy. What should you configure?
Answer Option 1: A Key Vault-backed container app secret resolved with a user-assigned managed identity, referenced from the environment variable with `secretref`
Explanation 1: Correct. Container Apps can define a secret whose value comes from a Key Vault secret URL, resolved using a managed identity assigned to the app, and the environment variable then references that secret by name with `secretref`. The material stays in the vault, the app configuration shows only the reference, and rotation is picked up without a code or image change.
Answer Option 2: A plain container app secret holding a copy of the key, referenced from the environment variable with `secretref`
Explanation 2: A plain secret does keep the value out of the environment-variable listing and out of the image, which is why it is tempting, but it stores a copy of the key in the container app resource. Rotation then requires updating that copy, which the requirement explicitly rules out.
Answer Option 3: An environment variable set directly to the key value, protected by restricting management-plane RBAC on the container app
Explanation 3: Putting the key straight into an environment variable exposes it to anyone who can read the app definition and to any diagnostic export of the configuration. Management-plane RBAC narrows who can look, but the secret is still stored in cleartext in the resource.
Answer Option 4: An init container that calls the Key Vault REST API at start-up and writes the key into a shared volume for the main container to read
Explanation 4: This hand-builds what the platform already provides, adding a bespoke component to maintain, a volume that now holds plaintext key material, and a failure mode at every start-up. Key Vault-backed secrets deliver the same outcome declaratively.
Overall Explanation: Use a Key Vault-backed container app secret resolved by a managed identity and reference it with `secretref`. The key never leaves the vault and rotation needs no redeploy.

Question: A healthcare document-ingestion service must reach Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL without any account keys in configuration. The platform team assigned the app's managed identity the Azure RBAC Contributor role on the Cosmos DB account and disabled local authentication. The app authenticates with `DefaultAzureCredential`, but every `create_item` call fails with a 403 stating the principal is not authorized to perform the data action. What is the cause?
Answer Option 1: Contributor is a control-plane role; the identity also needs a Cosmos DB data-plane role assignment such as Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor
Explanation 1: Correct. Cosmos DB separates control-plane Azure RBAC (managing the account, containers, throughput) from data-plane role-based access control over items. Contributor lets the identity manage resources but grants no item read or write actions, so a data-plane role definition such as Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor must be assigned to the principal at the account scope.
Answer Option 2: DefaultAzureCredential cannot be used with Cosmos DB, so the app must acquire a token for the account scope manually and pass it as a raw string
Explanation 2: DefaultAzureCredential is precisely what the Cosmos DB SDK expects for token-based auth — you pass the credential object as `credential=`. The failure is an authorization decision, not a credential-type problem, and hand-rolling token acquisition would produce the same 403.
Answer Option 3: Disabling local authentication blocks the SDK's data plane entirely, so writes must go through the control plane or a private endpoint
Explanation 3: Disabling local auth only turns off key-based access; token-based data-plane access continues to work and is the entire point of the configuration. The request reached the data plane and was evaluated, which is why a 403 rather than a connection error was returned.
Answer Option 4: The managed identity has not been granted the Reader role on the resource group, which Cosmos DB requires before evaluating any data-plane request
Explanation 4: Reader on the resource group is another control-plane assignment and adds no item-level permissions. Cosmos DB does not chain data-plane authorization off resource-group RBAC, so this would leave the 403 exactly as it is.
Overall Explanation: Cosmos DB has two independent permission systems: Azure RBAC for the account and a separate data-plane role model for items. A keyless app needs a data-plane role assignment such as Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor; Contributor alone yields a 403 on every item operation.

Question: A support-ticket search screen runs `SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.tenantId = @t ORDER BY c.priority DESC, c.updatedAt DESC` against Cosmos DB for NoSQL and fails with an error stating the ORDER BY query does not have a corresponding composite index. Which two changes are required to make the query succeed? (Choose two.)
Answer Option 1: Add a composite index to the container's indexing policy containing /priority and /updatedAt as its two paths
Explanation 1: Correct. Multi-property ORDER BY in Cosmos DB for NoSQL is only serviceable from a composite index that covers the sorted properties. Adding a composite index entry listing /priority and /updatedAt is the first half of the fix.
Answer Option 2: Define the composite index paths in the same order and with directions matching the ORDER BY clause, or its exact inverse
Explanation 2: Correct. Composite indexes are order- and direction-sensitive: the definition must list the paths in the same sequence as the ORDER BY and with matching directions, or with every direction flipped, which the engine can read backwards. A composite index of (/priority ASC, /updatedAt DESC) would not serve this query.
Answer Option 3: Increase the container's provisioned throughput so the sort can be completed within the request's RU allowance
Explanation 3: This misreads a definition error as a capacity error. The query is rejected before execution because no index can serve it, so no amount of provisioned RU/s changes the outcome — the failure is not a 429.
Answer Option 4: Add /priority and /updatedAt to includedPaths as separate range indexes, which together satisfy the multi-property sort
Explanation 4: Range indexes on individual properties serve filters and single-property sorts, and both paths are already indexed under the default policy — which is why the error still appears. Cosmos DB cannot combine two independent range indexes to satisfy a two-property ORDER BY.
Overall Explanation: A multi-property ORDER BY requires a composite index over exactly those paths, defined in the same order with matching directions or their full inverse. Separate range indexes cannot be combined to satisfy it, and extra throughput does not address a missing-index error.

Question: An analytics endpoint runs `SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.status = 'open' AND c.assignee = @user` over a Cosmos DB for NoSQL container partitioned on `/tenantId` that holds 900 physical partitions. Each call costs about 480 RUs and takes 1.4 seconds, even though it returns 12 documents. The calling service always knows the tenant. What is the most effective change?
Answer Option 1: Include the tenant in the predicate and pass `partition_key=tenant_id` to `query_items` so the query is routed to a single partition
Explanation 1: Correct. Without the partition key the query is a cross-partition fan-out: the gateway must ask all 900 physical partitions and merge results, and RU cost and latency scale with partitions touched rather than documents returned. Scoping the query to one partition value collapses it to a single-partition query with a fraction of the RU charge.
Answer Option 2: Set max_item_count to 12 so the SDK stops fetching pages once the requested number of documents has been produced
Explanation 2: max_item_count controls page size, not fan-out. The engine still contacts every partition to determine which documents match, so the dominant cost — 900 partition round trips — remains, and small pages can even increase the number of round trips.
Answer Option 3: Add a composite index on /status and /assignee so the two equality predicates can be evaluated from a single index lookup
Explanation 3: Composite indexes serve multi-property ORDER BY, not multiple equality filters, and both properties are already indexed by the default policy. Even a perfectly indexed predicate must still be evaluated on every partition when the partition key is absent.
Answer Option 4: Enable the container's integrated cache so repeated executions of this query are served without re-reading from the partitions
Explanation 4: The integrated cache can help identical repeated reads within its window, but it masks the design flaw rather than fixing it, does nothing for first-time or varied user filters, and requires dedicated gateway provisioning.
Overall Explanation: Queries that omit the partition key fan out to every physical partition, so RU charge and latency scale with partition count rather than result size. Passing the known tenant as the partition key routes the query to one partition and eliminates the scatter-gather.
Domain: Develop AI solutions by using Azure data management services

Question: A multi-tenant RAG service queries `SELECT TOP 10 c.id, c.text, VectorDistance(c.embedding, @q) AS score FROM c ORDER BY VectorDistance(c.embedding, @q)` against a container partitioned on `/tenantId`. Retrieval costs about 950 RUs per request and sometimes surfaces chunks belonging to a different tenant. What should the team change?
Answer Option 1: Add `WHERE c.tenantId = @tenant` and pass the tenant as the partition key so the vector search is scoped to that tenant's partition
Explanation 1: Correct. Without a tenant predicate the query is an unscoped cross-partition vector search: it fans out over every tenant's data, which explains both the RU charge and the leakage of other tenants' chunks. Filtering on tenantId and supplying it as the partition key restricts the search to one partition and makes isolation a property of the query, not of post-processing.
Answer Option 2: Sort on the `score` alias instead of repeating the VectorDistance expression, which lets the engine reuse the computed distance
Explanation 2: Reusing the alias is a reasonable style choice but does not change what the query scans; the engine still evaluates distance for candidate documents across all partitions. It addresses neither the cost nor, more importantly, the tenant-isolation defect.
Answer Option 3: Raise TOP to 50 and filter the tenant's chunks in application code before passing the surviving results to the model
Explanation 3: Over-fetching and filtering in application code is post-filtering: it still pays to search every tenant's vectors, and it can return fewer than 10 tenant-relevant chunks when the global top 50 is dominated by other tenants. Correctness that depends on over-fetching is not correctness.
Answer Option 4: Switch the distance function in the query to Euclidean, which returns better-separated scores and avoids cross-tenant matches
Explanation 4: The distance function must match the one declared in the container's vector embedding policy and reflects how the embedding model was trained; switching it degrades relevance. Distance metric has no bearing on which tenant's documents are eligible for retrieval.
Overall Explanation: Scope vector search with a tenant predicate and the matching partition key. An unscoped VectorDistance ORDER BY fans out across all partitions, driving RU cost up and allowing other tenants' chunks into the result set; post-filtering in application code fixes neither.

Question: A vector index in Azure AI Search is kept in step with a Cosmos DB for NoSQL container by a change feed processor running in latest-version mode. Newly created and edited documents are reflected within seconds, but documents deleted from Cosmos DB remain searchable indefinitely. What is the most appropriate remedy?
Answer Option 1: Replace hard deletes with a soft-delete flag plus TTL, so the deletion surfaces as an update the processor can act on
Explanation 1: Correct. In latest-version mode the change feed emits creates and updates but not deletes, so a hard delete is invisible to the consumer. Marking the item as deleted — an update the processor sees — and letting TTL remove the tombstone afterwards is the standard pattern for propagating deletions downstream.
Answer Option 2: Reduce the processor's poll interval so it observes the deletion before the document is physically removed from the container
Explanation 2: Polling faster does not help because deletes are never written to the latest-version feed at all; there is no window in which the processor could catch them. This treats a semantic gap as a timing race.
Answer Option 3: Enable the container's integrated cache and invalidate it on delete, which propagates removals to downstream consumers
Explanation 3: The integrated cache is a read-path optimisation for queries and point reads inside Cosmos DB. It has no channel to downstream systems and no interaction with the change feed, so invalidating it changes nothing in the search index.
Answer Option 4: Rebuild the entire search index on a nightly schedule, which is the only supported way to remove documents from a downstream store
Explanation 4: A nightly rebuild is a heavyweight workaround that leaves deleted documents searchable for up to a day and is not the only option. Soft deletes, or switching the feed to all versions and deletes mode, give near-real-time removal.
Overall Explanation: Latest-version change feed does not emit deletes, so hard-deleted documents never reach downstream consumers. Use a soft-delete flag with TTL so the removal arrives as an update, or switch to all versions and deletes mode.

Question: A nightly job re-embeds a corpus by running `SELECT id, chunk_text FROM chunks` over 4.2 million rows in Azure Database for PostgreSQL and iterating the result in Python. The container is killed by the orchestrator for exceeding its 2 GB memory limit before the loop produces its first embedding. What is the correct change to the data-access code?
Answer Option 1: Use a server-side (named) cursor and iterate it in batches so only a bounded window of rows is materialized in the client
Explanation 1: Correct. A client-side cursor pulls the entire result set into client memory before the first row is yielded, which is exactly the observed behaviour. A named cursor keeps the result set on the server and fetches it in configurable batches, so client memory stays bounded regardless of row count.
Answer Option 2: Add `LIMIT 100000` to the query and rerun the job repeatedly until a run returns fewer than 100,000 rows
Explanation 2: Bare LIMIT without a stable ordering and offset key gives no guarantee about which rows are returned, so runs can repeat and skip rows. Keyset pagination on id could work, but it is more code and more round trips than simply streaming with a server-side cursor.
Answer Option 3: Raise the container memory limit to 8 GB, since a 4.2 million row result set is inherently large and must be held in memory
Explanation 3: This buys headroom rather than fixing the pattern, and the corpus will keep growing — 8 GB merely moves the failure. It also wastes memory on rows the job processes one at a time and then discards.
Answer Option 4: Wrap the query in a read-only transaction with repeatable read isolation so PostgreSQL streams rows without buffering them
Explanation 4: Isolation level controls visibility of concurrent changes, not how the driver buffers rows. A repeatable-read transaction with a client-side cursor would consume exactly the same memory.
Overall Explanation: Client-side cursors materialize the whole result set before yielding a row. Use a server-side named cursor with a batch size so memory stays bounded, rather than raising limits or paginating with an unordered LIMIT.

Question: A team migrates from a 1536-dimension embedding model to one producing 3072 dimensions and stores the result in `embedding vector(3072)` on Azure Database for PostgreSQL. `CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)` fails because the column exceeds the dimension limit for an HNSW index over the vector type. Which option preserves the new model's output while enabling an approximate index?
Answer Option 1: Store the column as `halfvec(3072)` and build the HNSW index with `halfvec_cosine_ops`, which supports a higher dimension ceiling
Explanation 1: Correct. pgvector's half-precision type stores each element in 16 bits, which both halves index size and raises the indexable dimension ceiling above what the full-precision vector type allows. Recall loss from half precision is typically small for text embeddings, so this keeps the model's full 3072 dimensions while making an HNSW index possible.
Answer Option 2: Keep `vector(3072)` and build an IVFFlat index instead, since IVFFlat has no dimension limit for indexed columns
Explanation 2: IVFFlat is subject to the same indexed-dimension ceiling as HNSW for the full-precision vector type, so swapping index types does not lift the limit. It would also be a poor fit for a corpus that keeps changing, since its lists are built from a snapshot of the data.
Answer Option 3: Truncate every embedding to its first 2000 elements before insert so the existing HNSW index definition succeeds
Explanation 3: Arbitrarily truncating an embedding discards learned dimensions and degrades relevance in ways that are hard to detect. Dimension reduction is only safe with a model explicitly trained to support it, or with a proper projection fitted on the data.
Answer Option 4: Split the embedding across two `vector(1536)` columns and index each half separately, then average the two distances
Explanation 4: Splitting a vector in half and averaging two distances is not equivalent to the original cosine distance and produces incorrect rankings. It also doubles index maintenance and query complexity for a result that no longer matches the model's geometry.
Overall Explanation: Use halfvec(3072) with halfvec_cosine_ops to index high-dimensional embeddings: half precision cuts storage in half and raises the indexable dimension limit, whereas truncating or splitting vectors corrupts the model's distance geometry.

Question: A retrieval endpoint backed by an HNSW index on Azure Database for PostgreSQL runs with `hnsw.ef_search = 400` and shows p95 latency of 130 ms against a 60 ms budget. An offline evaluation reports recall@10 of 0.995, while the product team states 0.95 is acceptable. CPU on the server is the bottleneck. What is the most direct tuning step?
Answer Option 1: Lower hnsw.ef_search toward 60–100 and re-measure recall, trading surplus recall for reduced per-query work
Explanation 1: Correct. ef_search sets how many candidates the graph traversal keeps, so it is the direct dial between recall and CPU cost per query. With recall 0.045 above requirement, reducing ef_search cuts the traversal work proportionally and is reversible and measurable without an index rebuild.
Answer Option 2: Rebuild the index with a larger `m` so the graph has more links and each query traverses it faster
Explanation 2: Raising m adds links per node, which increases index size, build time and memory footprint and generally increases traversal work per query rather than reducing it. It is a recall-oriented parameter, and it requires a full rebuild to change.
Answer Option 3: Increase the server's storage size to raise provisioned IOPS and shorten index page reads
Explanation 3: The bottleneck is stated to be CPU, and a well-sized HNSW index is served largely from memory. Buying IOPS addresses a storage bottleneck that the evidence does not support.
Answer Option 4: Add `LIMIT 10` to the query if it is missing, so the index stops searching once ten neighbours are found
Explanation 4: LIMIT bounds the rows returned but the traversal breadth is governed by ef_search, which must be at least the limit; a query returning ten rows with ef_search 400 still explores 400 candidates. This misattributes the cost to result size.
Overall Explanation: hnsw.ef_search is the query-time recall/latency dial. With recall well above the requirement and CPU saturated, lowering ef_search and re-measuring is the direct fix; raising m or buying IOPS addresses different bottlenecks.

Question: After creating `CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops)` on Azure Database for PostgreSQL, retrieval latency is unchanged at 2.3 seconds for a 5 million row table. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the production query `ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 10` shows a parallel sequential scan followed by a top-N sort, with no index scan. What is the cause?
Answer Option 1: The index operator class does not match the query's distance operator, so rebuild it with vector_cosine_ops to serve `<=>`
Explanation 1: Correct. A pgvector index is built for one distance function through its operator class: vector_l2_ops serves `<->`, vector_cosine_ops serves `<=>`, and vector_ip_ops serves `<#>`. Because the query uses cosine distance and the index was built for L2, no index can satisfy the ordering and the planner falls back to a scan plus sort.
Answer Option 2: The planner has stale statistics for the chunks table, so running ANALYZE will make it choose the vector index
Explanation 2: Stale statistics change cost estimates between viable plans, but here the index is not a candidate at all for this operator. ANALYZE would leave the plan exactly as it is.
Answer Option 3: HNSW indexes are only used when the query includes an explicit `WHERE` clause that narrows the candidate rows
Explanation 3: This is backwards: an ANN index is most naturally used for pure ordering queries, and adding a WHERE clause tends to complicate rather than enable index use. Nothing in pgvector requires a filter for the index to be considered.
Answer Option 4: The LIMIT is too small for the planner to consider an index scan worthwhile, so raising it to 100 will switch the plan
Explanation 4: Small limits favour index-driven top-k, not disfavour it; raising LIMIT increases the work an index scan must do. The plan is a scan because no compatible index exists, so the limit value is irrelevant.
Overall Explanation: pgvector operator classes bind an index to one distance function: vector_cosine_ops for `<=>`, vector_l2_ops for `<->`, vector_ip_ops for `<#>`. A mismatch makes the index unusable and leaves a sequential scan plus sort in the plan.

Question: An Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server hosting an embedding store runs on Premium SSD storage sized at 128 GiB. Bulk ingestion of 3 million chunks stalls with heavy write waits, and metrics show the storage IOPS metric pinned at its ceiling while only 60 GiB of the disk is used. The team does not want to pay for capacity it will not consume. Which option best resolves the throttling?
Answer Option 1: Move the server to Premium SSD v2, where provisioned IOPS and throughput are configured independently of the disk size
Explanation 1: Correct. On Premium SSD the IOPS ceiling is tied to the provisioned disk size, so the only way to get more IOPS is to buy capacity you do not need. Premium SSD v2 decouples the two, letting the team raise IOPS and throughput while keeping the allocated size close to actual usage — exactly the stated constraint.
Answer Option 2: Enable storage autogrow so the volume expands automatically once ingestion pushes utilisation past its threshold
Explanation 2: Autogrow protects against running out of space, which is not the problem: 60 GiB of 128 GiB is in use. Growth would only raise IOPS as a side effect of buying more capacity, which is precisely the cost the team wants to avoid.
Answer Option 3: Increase the number of vCores, since IOPS limits on flexible server are derived from the compute tier
Explanation 3: On flexible server, storage IOPS limits come from the storage tier and provisioned size rather than from vCore count, so scaling compute leaves the ceiling in place. It would add cost while the writes continue to queue on storage.
Answer Option 4: Split the ingestion into smaller transactions so each commit writes fewer pages and stays below the IOPS ceiling
Explanation 4: Smaller transactions change commit granularity, not the total number of pages that must be written; the same data still has to reach storage. It can even increase total I/O through more frequent WAL flushes.
Overall Explanation: Premium SSD ties IOPS to provisioned disk size, so an I/O-bound ingestion forces over-provisioning of capacity. Premium SSD v2 lets IOPS and throughput be set independently of size; autogrow, vCores and smaller transactions do not lift the ceiling.

Question: After routing a Python service through the built-in PgBouncer on Azure Database for PostgreSQL in transaction pooling mode, the team sees intermittent errors about prepared statements already existing, and a `SET statement_timeout` issued once per connection stops taking effect for later queries. What is the correct explanation and adjustment?
Answer Option 1: Transaction pooling assigns a different server connection per transaction, so client-side prepared statements and session-level SET must be disabled or reissued per transaction
Explanation 1: Correct. In transaction pooling mode a client is bound to a server connection only for the duration of a transaction, so anything that lives in session state — named prepared statements, session GUCs set with SET, temporary tables, advisory locks — is not guaranteed to be there next time. The fix is to disable client-side statement preparation (for example by turning off the driver's prepare threshold) or set parameters per transaction, or to use session pooling where session state is required.
Answer Option 2: The pooler's pool size is too small, so connections are being reused before their prepared statements have been deallocated
Explanation 2: Pool size affects queuing and wait time, not the semantics of session state. Enlarging the pool would leave prepared statements just as likely to be created on a connection that already has them, since assignment is still per transaction.
Answer Option 3: Prepared statements are unsupported by Azure Database for PostgreSQL, so all queries must be sent as literal SQL strings
Explanation 3: PostgreSQL supports prepared statements fully, and the service worked before the pooler was introduced. The conflict is with transaction-level multiplexing, not with the database's capabilities.
Answer Option 4: The application is missing an explicit BEGIN, so PostgreSQL runs each statement in its own implicit transaction and discards session state
Explanation 4: PostgreSQL does apply implicit transactions to standalone statements, but that has always been true and does not discard session GUCs on a direct connection. The behaviour changed only when the pooler was introduced, which points at pooling mode.
Overall Explanation: Transaction-mode pooling rebinds the client to a different server connection each transaction, so named prepared statements, session SET, temp tables and advisory locks are unreliable. Disable client-side preparation and set parameters per transaction, or use session pooling when session state is genuinely required.

Question: A pricing assistant caches catalogue lookups in Azure Managed Redis with a 30-minute TTL. After merchandisers change a price in the system of record, customers keep receiving the old price for up to half an hour, and the business requires the change to be visible within seconds. Which two changes achieve that? (Choose two.)
Answer Option 1: Delete or overwrite the affected cache keys as part of the same workflow that commits the price change
Explanation 1: Correct. TTL bounds worst-case staleness but says nothing about when the source actually changes; active invalidation on write is what converts a 30-minute window into a sub-second one. Publishing the invalidation from the same workflow that commits the change keeps cache and source of record coupled at the point where they can diverge.
Answer Option 2: Include a version or updated-at marker in the cache key so a price change makes previously cached entries unreachable
Explanation 2: Correct. Versioned keys make invalidation implicit: a write that bumps the version means every subsequent read looks up a key that does not exist yet, so it misses and repopulates. Stale entries simply age out under their own TTL and can never be served again.
Answer Option 3: Rely on the maxmemory eviction policy to remove outdated entries once memory pressure builds
Explanation 3: Eviction is a memory-pressure mechanism with no relationship to data correctness — it removes whichever keys the policy selects, which may well be fresh ones while stale entries survive. Depending on it for freshness gives you no bound at all.
Answer Option 4: Enable data persistence on the cache so restarts do not reintroduce values that were already superseded
Explanation 4: Persistence controls whether data survives a restart; it neither detects source changes nor removes outdated values. If anything, persisting stale prices makes them survive a restart that would previously have cleared them.
Overall Explanation: Bound staleness with TTL, but eliminate it by invalidating on write: delete or overwrite affected keys in the same workflow that commits the change, or embed a version in the key so old entries become unreachable. Eviction policy and persistence address neither.

Question: A multi-tenant SaaS assistant uses one semantic cache in Azure Managed Redis for all customers, storing prompt embedding, answer text and a `tenantId` field per entry. A security review finds that a question asked by tenant A can return an answer generated from tenant B's private documents. Which design change resolves this?
Answer Option 1: Scope every similarity search to the caller's tenant with a tenant filter in the query, and include the tenant in the key prefix
Explanation 1: Correct. Storing tenantId on the entry is useless unless the retrieval path enforces it, so the tenant must be part of the query — a filter combined with the vector search — and reflected in the key prefix so keyspaces are separable for both lookup and bulk invalidation. Isolation has to be enforced where matching happens, not merely recorded.
Answer Option 2: Encrypt the cached answer text at rest so that entries belonging to other tenants cannot be read if returned
Explanation 2: Encryption at rest protects against someone reading the underlying storage; it does nothing when the application itself decrypts and returns an entry it should never have matched. The failure is an authorization defect, not a storage-confidentiality one.
Answer Option 3: Reduce the cache TTL to five minutes so cross-tenant answers can only be served for a short window
Explanation 3: Shortening the TTL narrows the exposure window but leaves cross-tenant answers reachable within it, which no security review would accept. Time-boxing a data-leak path is not the same as closing it.
Answer Option 4: Store one embedding per tenant-agnostic canonical question so answers are generic and safe to share
Explanation 4: Forcing generic answers throws away the tenant-specific grounding that makes the assistant useful, and it does not prevent tenant-specific content from being cached in the first place. It solves the leak by removing the feature.
Overall Explanation: Enforce tenancy where matching happens: filter similarity searches by tenant and prefix keys per tenant so keyspaces are separable. A tenantId field that no query checks provides no isolation, and encryption or short TTLs do not close the path.

Question: A customer-service agent keeps per-conversation state — recent turns, the active tool context and a summary — in Azure Managed Redis so any stateless API replica can continue a conversation. The team must keep memory bounded while ensuring a completed conversation can still be reviewed months later for quality assurance. Which two practices should they adopt? (Choose two.)
Answer Option 1: Keep each conversation in its own key or hash with an expiry that is refreshed on every turn, so idle conversations age out
Explanation 1: Correct. A per-conversation key with an expiry refreshed on each turn implements a sliding session window: active conversations stay resident and abandoned ones release memory automatically, without a sweeper job. It also keeps reads and writes scoped to a single key, which is what stateless replicas need for fast resumption.
Answer Option 2: Persist the completed transcript to a durable store at the end of the conversation, treating Redis as working state only
Explanation 2: Correct. Redis is working state that can be expired, evicted or lost across scaling and failover, so anything needed months later must be written to a durable store. Persisting the transcript on completion separates the latency-sensitive live path from the long-term record.
Answer Option 3: Remove expiry from conversation keys and rely on the cache's eviction policy to reclaim memory when needed
Explanation 3: Without expiry, abandoned conversations accumulate indefinitely, and eviction then discards keys chosen by policy — quite possibly active conversations — producing user-visible state loss at the worst moment. Eviction is a memory-pressure valve, not a retention design.
Answer Option 4: Store the entire transcript in one string value and rewrite the whole value on every turn to keep reads simple
Explanation 4: Rewriting a growing transcript on every turn makes each write cost proportional to conversation length and produces large values that block other work as they are serialized. A hash or list of turns lets the agent append and read the recent window cheaply.
Overall Explanation: Give each conversation its own key with an expiry refreshed per turn so idle sessions age out, and persist the completed transcript to a durable store because Redis can expire, evict or lose it. Relying on eviction or rewriting one giant value creates both memory and correctness problems.

Question: A retail platform publishes a ProductUpdated message for every catalog change. Three independent back-end services must each act on every message: an embedding refresher, a price-index rebuilder, and an audit archiver. Today all three read from one Service Bus queue, and each message is processed by whichever service receives it first, so the other two never see it. What is the correct fix?
Answer Option 1: Replace the queue with a Service Bus topic and give each service its own subscription so all three receive an independent copy of every message
Explanation 1: Correct. A queue is a competing-consumers construct: one message goes to exactly one receiver. A topic with three subscriptions gives each service a durable, independently tracked copy, with its own delivery count, its own dead-letter queue, and its own backlog — which is precisely the durable publish-subscribe shape this scenario needs.
Answer Option 2: Keep the single queue but have each service peek messages instead of receiving them, so a message stays available to the other two services
Explanation 2: Peeking returns messages without locking them, so nothing is ever removed and the same messages are read forever. Peek is a diagnostic and browsing operation, not a delivery mode: it gives you no lock, no completion, and no way to track which service has finished which message.
Answer Option 3: Keep the single queue and enable sessions, assigning each service a distinct session id so each one gets its own stream of messages
Explanation 3: Sessions group related messages so they are handled in order by a single consumer; the session id comes from the producer's partitioning intent, not from consumer identity. Assigning a session per service would just split the single stream three ways — each message still lands in only one session and therefore reaches only one service.
Answer Option 4: Keep the single queue and have the publisher send three copies of every message, one tagged for each consuming service
Explanation 4: Publisher-side fan-out works only until the fourth consumer appears, and it puts routing knowledge in the producer: adding, removing, or filtering a consumer becomes a code change and a redeploy. Topics move that routing into the broker, where a new subscription is a configuration change with no producer impact.
Overall Explanation: When several independent services each need every message, use a Service Bus topic with one subscription per service. A single queue distributes each message to exactly one competing consumer, which is why two of the three services never see it.

Question: An overnight enrichment queue has accumulated 812 messages in its dead-letter queue. Sampling shows two causes: about 90 percent were malformed payloads that raise a parse error on every delivery until MaxDeliveryCount was exhausted, and the rest expired while a downstream service was offline. The team needs a supportable dead-letter strategy. Which two actions are appropriate? (Choose two.)
Answer Option 1: Build a triage consumer that receives from the queue's dead-letter sub-queue and reads DeadLetterReason and DeadLetterErrorDescription to classify each message
Explanation 1: Correct. The dead-letter queue is a real sub-queue you read with an ordinary receiver, and Service Bus stamps DeadLetterReason and DeadLetterErrorDescription on each message. A triage consumer that reads those properties can separate poison payloads that need a code or data fix from transient failures that can simply be resubmitted.
Answer Option 2: Explicitly dead-letter a message with a reason as soon as the payload fails schema validation, instead of letting it burn through ten deliveries first
Explanation 2: Correct. A payload that cannot be parsed will never succeed, so letting it consume the full delivery budget wastes ten receives, ten model-adjacent code paths, and roughly ten times the latency before it lands where it belongs. Calling dead_letter_message with an explicit reason moves a known-unrecoverable message aside immediately and records why.
Answer Option 3: Raise MaxDeliveryCount on the queue to 200 so malformed messages have more chances to succeed before being dead-lettered
Explanation 3: This scales the wrong dimension: a deterministic parse failure fails identically on delivery 200 as on delivery 1, so a higher delivery count only multiplies wasted work and delays discovery. Delivery count exists to absorb transient faults, not to grind against permanently invalid data.
Answer Option 4: Disable dead-lettering on the queue so that failing messages stay in the active queue and are retried indefinitely
Explanation 4: Turning dead-lettering off removes the quarantine that keeps poison messages from blocking the pipeline: they return to the active queue forever, consuming receiver capacity and hiding the failure signal. The dead-letter queue is the mechanism that makes bad messages visible instead of endlessly recycled.
Overall Explanation: Treat the dead-letter sub-queue as a first-class endpoint — receive from it and classify on DeadLetterReason — and dead-letter known-invalid payloads immediately rather than exhausting MaxDeliveryCount. Raising delivery counts or disabling dead-lettering only hides poison messages.

Question: A storage account raises Blob Created events for every upload across many containers. A reindexing function should run only for blobs written under the documents/incoming/ prefix and only when the event data's contentType is application/pdf. Today the function receives every blob event and discards about 95 percent of them in code. What is the best change?
Answer Option 1: Configure the event subscription with a subject filter for the documents/incoming/ prefix plus an advanced filter on data.contentType, so Event Grid delivers only matching events
Explanation 1: Correct. Event Grid filters at the subscription, so non-matching events are never delivered and never billed as handler executions. Subject filtering handles the path prefix and advanced filters evaluate fields inside the event payload such as data.contentType, which together express exactly the 5 percent the function cares about.
Answer Option 2: Keep the broad subscription and move the discard logic to the top of the handler so the function returns earlier on non-matching events
Explanation 2: Returning early still pays for delivery, a function invocation, cold-start risk, and log volume for every one of the discarded events. It optimizes the handler's inner loop while leaving the real waste — twenty times more invocations than necessary — completely in place.
Answer Option 3: Create a separate storage account for PDF uploads so that the existing subscription naturally receives only relevant events
Explanation 3: Restructuring storage to encode routing is a heavy, disruptive answer to a filtering problem, and it breaks down the moment a second routing dimension such as content type or tenant appears. Subscription filters express the same intent as configuration, without moving any data.
Answer Option 4: Subscribe to the events with a Service Bus topic in between and write a SQL rule on the subscription that inspects the blob path
Explanation 4: Interposing a Service Bus topic adds a hop, a second broker, and a second set of failure modes purely to run a rule that Event Grid can already evaluate itself. It is the right pattern when you also need durable buffering or competing consumers, not when the requirement is simply to stop delivering irrelevant events.
Overall Explanation: Express routing as Event Grid subscription filters: subject prefix for the path and an advanced filter on data.contentType. Filtering in handler code still pays the delivery, invocation, and logging cost for every event you throw away.

Question: A worker calls a partner API that returns 503 with a Retry-After of about 90 seconds during the partner's nightly window. Today the worker abandons the message on failure, so Service Bus redelivers it within milliseconds; the message churns through its whole delivery budget in under a second and dead-letters, even though it would have succeeded a couple of minutes later. What is the best fix?
Answer Option 1: On a transient failure, complete the message and re-send a copy with scheduled_enqueue_time_utc set past the retry window, carrying an attempt counter in the application properties
Explanation 1: Correct. Abandon makes a message immediately visible again, which is why the delivery budget evaporates in under a second. Scheduling a fresh copy for a future enqueue time turns redelivery into a real backoff: the message leaves the active queue, stops consuming receiver capacity, and reappears after the partner window, with the attempt counter carrying the retry state.
Answer Option 2: Keep abandoning the message but raise MaxDeliveryCount to 500 so the churn eventually outlasts the partner's maintenance window
Explanation 2: A larger delivery budget still gets consumed at the same millisecond cadence, so this mostly converts a fast failure into a burst of hundreds of pointless receives and partner calls. It treats the symptom — dead-lettering — while leaving the actual defect, retry with no delay, untouched.
Answer Option 3: Have the worker sleep for 90 seconds inside the message handler and retry the partner call in place before completing the message
Explanation 3: Sleeping inside the handler holds the message lock and an entire concurrency slot idle for 90 seconds, so a queue of such messages stalls the whole consumer pool. It also risks exceeding the lock without renewal, which reintroduces duplicate processing on top of the throughput loss.
Answer Option 4: Set the queue's lock duration to 90 seconds so an abandoned message cannot be redelivered until the partner has recovered
Explanation 4: Lock duration bounds how long a receiver may hold a message; abandon explicitly releases the lock early, so the lock setting has no effect on how quickly an abandoned message returns. The delay has to be expressed on the message's enqueue time, not on the lock.
Overall Explanation: Abandon returns a message instantly, so it is not backoff. Re-send with scheduled_enqueue_time_utc beyond the retry window and track attempts on the message, which frees consumer capacity and preserves the delivery budget for genuine failures.

Question: A publisher that submits reindex commands sometimes retries a send after a network timeout even though the broker actually accepted the original. The team wants Service Bus itself to discard the second copy when the same logical command is submitted twice within a ten-minute window. What must they configure?
Answer Option 1: Create the queue with duplicate detection enabled and have the publisher set a deterministic message_id derived from the command's business key
Explanation 1: Correct. Duplicate detection compares the MessageId of incoming messages against those seen inside the detection history window, so it only works if the publisher supplies an id that is stable across retries. Deriving message_id from the command's business key makes the retried send an exact repeat that the broker can recognize and drop.
Answer Option 2: Enable sessions on the queue and set session_id to the command's business key so the broker discards repeats within the session
Explanation 2: Sessions provide ordering and single-receiver affinity for a group of related messages; they do not de-duplicate. Two identical commands sharing a session_id would both be delivered, just in order, which is not the behavior the team asked for.
Answer Option 3: Enable duplicate detection on the queue and rely on the broker's default message id, which Service Bus assigns per send
Explanation 3: A broker- or client-generated MessageId is different on every send, so a retried command carries a brand-new id and looks like a new message. Duplicate detection would be enabled and would faithfully find no duplicates — the classic reason this feature appears not to work.
Answer Option 4: Set the consumer's receive mode to peek-lock and complete each message, which makes the broker reject a later send of the same body
Explanation 4: Peek-lock and completion describe how a consumer takes ownership of a message; they have no influence on what the broker accepts at send time. The broker never compares message bodies, only MessageId within the detection window.
Overall Explanation: Enable duplicate detection at queue creation and have the publisher set a deterministic message_id from the business key — the broker matches on MessageId, never on body. Sessions order messages, they do not de-duplicate.
